extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of political philosophy; activists considering civil disobedience; people who want to read or redistribute Project Gutenberg eBooks
extracted.subtask_description: Henry David Thoreau's essay arguing when and how individuals should refuse allegiance to unjust governments (civil disobedience), plus the Project Gutenberg license terms attached to the eBook. The page contains prescriptive principles for resisting unjust laws and explicit redistribution requirements for Project Gutenberg works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of conscience over law
rubrics_metrics.description: A citizen must not resign his conscience to the legislator; the only obligation one has a right to assume is to do at any time what one thinks right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau argues repeatedly that conscience, not law or majority rule, should determine action. He contrasts 'respect for the law' with respect for the right, warning that law often makes people agents of injustice. Example: refusing to follow laws that uphold slavery or an unjust war.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to resist (threshold for disobedience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist the government when its tyranny or inefficiency are great and unendurable—specifically when injustice is organized (e.g., slavery, aggressive war).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau cites slavery and the Mexican war as concrete cases where honest men should rebel rather than wait for majority action. He rejects purely expediency-based calculations (Paley) for these cases and holds that justice must be done 'cost what it may.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Act from principle, not expediency
rubrics_metrics.description: Action must spring from principle—the perception and performance of right—rather than calculations of convenience, probability of success, or majority approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voting, petitioning, or waiting for the majority are criticized as insufficient; moral action may require immediate transgression of unjust laws despite personal cost. Thoreau's anti-Paley argument: some moral obligations cannot be reduced to profit/loss computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdraw practical support from unjust institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Effectively withdraw both personal and property support from a government that commits injustice (e.g., do not pay taxes that fund slavery or war).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau recommends refusing to give the government money or other resources that make one complicit. He models this by refusing to pay poll-tax for years and describes refusal to pay as a principal mode of protest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resignation or refusal by public officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Public officers who do not wish to be instruments of injustice should resign rather than continue to enforce unjust laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau advises that when a subject refuses allegiance, the corresponding officer's resignation completes the revolution—resignation is offered as a practical remedy for conscientious officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept the penalty (willingness to suffer)
rubrics_metrics.description: A just person should be willing to accept legal penalties (imprisonment, seizure) rather than cooperate with injustice; prison can be the honorable place for a just man under an unjust government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau narrates his own one-night imprisonment after refusing to pay taxes and frames imprisonment as morally significant and educational. Accepting punishment is a form of nonviolent witness that can highlight injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonviolent 'counter-friction' as tactic
rubrics_metrics.description: Let your life be a peaceful counter-friction to stop the machine of government that perpetrates wrongs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau advocates nonviolent resistance—refusing to be the government's agent, withdrawing cooperation, and using moral pressure (not physical violence) to clog the machinery of injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: ‘Majority of one’ — moral courage has disproportionate power
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual who is morally right constitutes a 'majority of one' and can have decisive moral influence; one honest person can effect real change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau asserts that reform often begins with the single well-done act; he gives the hypothetical that one honest man ceasing to hold slaves and enduring imprisonment could abolish slavery through example and moral pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on voting alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Casting a vote is morally weak if it's merely a token act; real commitment requires casting your whole influence and not leaving the right to the chance of majority rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau compares voting to gaming; he criticizes those who treat voting as sufficient without taking direct, principled action. He argues that 'only his vote can hasten the abolition of slavery who asserts his own freedom by his vote'—meaning action beyond the ballot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid indirect complicity (trace effects of allegiance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful of how allegiance and money are used: even indirect support (commerce, taxes) can make one complicit in state injustice and should be avoided when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau stresses tracing the effects of your allegiance—if your dollar buys a musket or funds slavery, you are complicit. He refuses to track the dollar's path in detail but insists on refusing the allegiance that produces those effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do justice regardless of cost
rubrics_metrics.description: When justice demands it, act even if the remedy will cost the people their existence as a political entity; moral duty can override considerations of collective survival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau claims that a people must cease to hold slaves and make unjust war 'though it cost them their existence as a people,' placing absolute moral duty above national preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissolve personal union with the state
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals should dissolve their personal union with the state when it is unjust—refuse allegiance, cease participation in state institutions, and withdraw from 'copartnership' with the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau asks reformers to 'withdraw their support, both in person and property, from the government' and likens the moral act to dissolving a partnership; practical acts include refusing taxes and other forms of civic cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicality critique: government as expedient and obstructive
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize government as an expedient that often obstructs the people's character and enterprise; distrust appeals to the government's inherent virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau argues governments rarely advance enterprises and sometimes impede them; he warns against cultivating respect for law over right and sees government as a machine that may need active counter-friction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target the proximate agents of state power
rubrics_metrics.description: Confront the immediate representatives or agents of the state (e.g., tax-gatherer) when withdrawing allegiance—treat action as personal and face-to-face where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau frames his refusal to pay tax as a direct encounter with 'the tax-gatherer'—practical civil disobedience involves clear, personal acts that communicate conscience to the agent enforcing unjust laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer personal moral usefulness over civic servility
rubrics_metrics.description: Be 'useful as a man'—do not submit to become a mere instrument of the state; preserve moral individuality rather than conforming to roles that avoid moral discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau distinguishes between those who serve the State with their bodies or heads (machines, mere professionals) and the few who serve with conscience; he urges men to be heroes/patriots rather than 'useful serving-man[s]'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break laws that require you to be agent of injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: If complying with a law makes you the agent of injustice to another person, you should break that law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau's rule: if the law requires you to be the agent of another's injury, it is your duty to disobey. He frames civil disobedience as a moral imperative in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imprisonment as moral instrument and pedagogical experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience of imprisonment can be revealing, non-degrading, and a mode of protest that clarifies one's relation to the community and state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau's prison narrative describes learning about the town, humanity of prisoners, and the symbolic force of being locked up for conscience—use imprisonment to demonstrate the state's limited power and to educate both self and community.
